title: When the Drop Falls
premise: Odile Voss, a sleepless interpreter haunted by a peace summit that ended in a massacre she may have mistranslated into existence, is summoned when a voiceprint — her own voice, recorded years ago — unlocks a black server in Tallinn containing proof the talks were sabotaged from within. Sent to extract Marek Sova, a defector who claims he can name the saboteur, Odile discovers Marek is bait in a trap designed to flush out everyone who remembers what really happened, including her. As hunters close in across three borders, Odile must decide whether survival means burying the truth again or speaking it aloud, at last, in her own words. The book ends with Odile testifying before an inquiry, trading her anonymity and safety for the truth — and sleeping through the night for the first time since the incident.
about_author: Oscar Yarrow is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent a decade in rooms where one wrong word could end a ceasefire. They write thrillers about people whose professions demand perfect neutrality — and what happens when neutrality fails.

chapters.title: The Hour Before Dawn
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In Geneva, Odile wakes at 3:14 a.m. again, rehearsing old interpretations in the dark. A flashback sketches the failed Meridian Summit and the bombing that killed eleven delegates. Emotional beat: guilt worn smooth by repetition, a life narrowed to insomnia and routine.

chapters.title: Voiceprint
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. An encrypted message arrives: a server in Tallinn has unlocked using a voice sample of Odile from 2019 — audio she never consented to record. Her handler, Ilsa Brandt, confirms someone is deliberately summoning her. Beat: dread sharpening into reluctant purpose.

chapters.title: What the Server Knew
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, with a brief interlude from the anonymous sender. The Tallinn files show the summit's security briefings were doctored — translated wrong on purpose, and the mistranslation traces back to Odile's own booth feed. Beat: vertigo; her guilt may be manufactured.

chapters.title: The Defector's Terms
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Brandt recruits Odile for an extraction: Marek Sova, a signals officer hiding in Riga, will only talk to the interpreter whose voice opened the server. Brandt omits that headquarters suspects a mole. Beat: complicity begins; Odile says yes to escape her own head.

chapters.title: Riga Rain
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Arriving under a cover identity as a trade delegate, Odile makes contact through a chess club dead-drop and meets Marek — younger than expected, terrified, precise. He tests her with a phrase only the real summit staff would know. Beat: wary alliance.

chapters.title: Marek's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Marek explains he kept copies of the tampered translation logs and names his contact inside the delegation: codename LANTERN. But he admits he doesn't know if LANTERN is the saboteur or another victim. Beat: the truth is layered; trust is a wager.

chapters.title: Tail
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Leaving the meet, Odile spots a surveillance pattern too clean to be accidental — they were allowed to connect. She and Marek run through the old town, splitting up at the market. Beat: adrenaline; the trap has teeth.

chapters.title: Safehouse Static
chapters.summary: Odile and Marek, alternating POV. Holed up in a safehouse, they reconstruct the summit timeline together; Odile realizes her 'mistranslation' was spliced from archived recordings of her voice. Someone built her guilt. Beat: fury replacing shame.

chapters.title: LANTERN
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Brandt receives orders to terminate the extraction if Sova's intel can't be verified — and recognizes LANTERN's cipher style as someone she trained. She burns a channel to buy Odile time. Beat: divided loyalty; the institution is not innocent.

chapters.title: The Ferry to Helsinki
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A smuggled crossing goes wrong when border drones flag Marek's biometrics. Odile uses her interpreter's ear to mimic a customs officer's cadence over comms and talk them past inspection. Beat: her skill, once her curse, becomes their weapon.

chapters.title: Helsinki, Half-Lit
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Waiting in a sauna district safehouse, Marek confesses he was coerced into planting the splice — his sister is held as leverage. Odile must weigh his confession against the mission. Beat: sympathy complicating judgment; no clean hands.

chapters.title: The Mole's Voice
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Analyzing the splice's audio artifacts, Odile identifies the second voice in the doctored recordings — a colleague from the summit, Elias Renner, presumed dead in the bombing. Beat: the dead man walking; grief weaponized.

chapters.title: Renner
chapters.summary: Elias Renner's POV (first appearance). Alive and working for the network that staged the massacre, Renner monitors the extraction, arguing to keep Odile alive because her testimony gives the cover story credibility. Beat: cold pragmatism; the antagonist humanized just enough.

chapters.title: Bait Confirmed
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile decodes Marek's ledger fully and understands: Marek was released on purpose; the whole extraction is theater to expose every survivor who doubts the official story. Telling Brandt means admitting she knew and continued. Beat: the price of survival comes due.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Headquarters moves to close the operation and silence both assets. Brandt goes rogue, sending Odile one word — RUN — before her access is revoked. Beat: betrayal by the institution; a lone ally's sacrifice.

chapters.title: Night Train South
chapters.summary: Odile and Marek, alternating POV. Fleeing toward Stockholm on a freight ferry, they plan to reach the inquiry's legal counsel directly rather than any intelligence service. Marek hesitates — his sister. Beat: hope with a hostage attached.

chapters.title: The Sister
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. A rendezvous to recover Marek's sister, Lena, is ambushed; Renner's team takes all three. In captivity, Renner offers Odile her old life back if she recants. Beat: temptation framed as mercy; the lowest point.

chapters.title: Interpretation
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In a locked room, Odile turns interrogator's tool against captor: she listens — to guards' radio chatter, to Renner's tells — and maps the building's rhythms. She engineers an escape during a shift change, getting Lena out while staying behind. Beat: agency reclaimed at personal cost.

chapters.title: What Odile Said
chapters.summary: Climax, Odile vs. Renner. Cornered, Odile forces Renner to admit the sabotage on a live open mic Brandt left running — using the exact phrasing of the original mistranslated briefing so the recording matches the archive. Renner is taken by his own network; the broadcast escapes. Beat: language as the decisive weapon.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Tallinn
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The recording reaches journalists and the inquiry; headquarters scrambles, Brandt resurfaces to shepherd evidence, and Marek and Lena go into protected witness status. Odile declines protection. Beat: exhale; consequences rippling outward.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Before the inquiry, Odile interprets nothing — she speaks for herself, naming the dead, the splice, and her own years of manufactured guilt. Renner's network begins to unravel publicly. Beat: catharsis; memory spoken plainly at last.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Odile's POV. Months later, Odile teaches interpretation in a small coastal town, visits the memorial, and sleeps until morning. A letter from Marek arrives with a chess move. Final beat: belonging chosen, not assigned; the price paid was worth it.
